claims.text: Variations in stacking-fault energy govern the mechanical-property differences between equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its lower-order FCC subsets.
Changing the Mn/Co ratio can reduce the stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation twinning.
Deformation twinning enhances strain hardening and ductility.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors dislocation glide over deformation twinning.
The investigated equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and selected quaternary and ternary subsets can be maintained as single-phase FCC materials.
Identical thermomechanical processing will produce sufficiently comparable grain structures and phase purity across the selected compositions.
Reducing Mn content in selected quaternary alloys will lower stacking-fault energy while preserving a single-phase FCC structure.
Twin density and morphology can serve as an indirect characterization of local stacking-fault energy.
Ab initio stacking-fault-energy calculations can independently corroborate the inferred stacking-fault-energy changes.
Altering the Mn/Co ratio changes the alloy's electronic environment, which in turn changes its stacking-fault energy.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys engineered for lower stacking-fault energy through reduced Mn will have greater deformation-twin density.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys engineered for lower stacking-fault energy will exhibit higher strain-hardening rates and improved ductility.
Alloys with higher stacking-fault energy will exhibit less twinning and lower ductility.
The proposed stacking-fault-energy relationship applies only while the alloys remain single-phase FCC and major microstructural variables such as grain size remain comparable.
Lattice distortion and segregation may confound the relationship between composition, stacking-fault energy, and mechanical behavior.
